messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 68
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: School Counselor
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 62

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Emotional Closeness: Someone getting emotionally close to me, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out, Avoid People: avoid other people, Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Emmett had been a school counselor for over three decades, dedicating his life to helping students navigate the ups and downs of adolescence. But on one fateful evening six years ago, Emmett's own life took a drastic turn when he was brutally assaulted by a stranger in a parking garage near his home. The attack left him with physical scars that would eventually heal, but the emotional wounds lingered. As Emmett recounts the event, it's clear that certain details remain etched in his mind like snapshots. He remembers the smell of antiseptic wafting from his attacker's clothes, a scent that now instantly transports him back to that terrifying moment. The hospital where he was taken after the assault has become a trigger as well; the sterile smell and fluorescent lights evoke an overwhelming sense of dread. But it's not just specific smells that unsettle Emmett – emotional closeness with others has also become a source of distress. As someone who had always prided himself on being empathetic and supportive, he now finds himself pulling away from loved ones, fearful of letting his guard down. His wife, in particular, feels the sting of this new distance. She's grown accustomed to Emmett's emotional unavailability, but it pains her to see him withdraw into himself. When memories of the assault resurface, Emmett is hit with a wave of terror that's just as intense as it was on the night of the attack. These recollections often come in fragmented flashes – a sudden piece of the puzzle dropping into place without warning – leaving him disoriented and breathless. It's as if his mind has created a patchwork quilt of memories, with some moments frozen in time like snapshots. To cope with these overwhelming feelings, Emmett has developed a few maladaptive strategies. He often dissociates deliberately, trying to leave his body or blank out the emotions that threaten to engulf him. This coping mechanism has become so automatic that he's started to notice its presence even in mundane situations – like when he's watching TV and suddenly feels himself "checking out." Emmett also finds solace in avoiding people, particularly those who might try to get close to him emotionally. As a school counselor, this has meant scaling back his involvement with students and colleagues alike, opting for more superficial relationships that don't risk exposing his vulnerability. The irony isn't lost on him – he's become a shadow of the empathetic professional he once was. Another trigger that catches Emmett off guard is the smell of alcohol. He recalls that his attacker reeked of booze that night, and now even a whiff of it sends him spiraling back into the darkness. As time has passed, these avoidance behaviors have taken their toll on Emmett's relationships and daily life. His wife feels increasingly isolated, and his job performance has begun to suffer as he becomes more withdrawn. It was only when his school principal expressed concern about his growing absence from meetings and student sessions that Emmett realized he needed help. Now, at 68, Emmett is seeking therapy in the hopes of breaking free from the shackles of his PTSD. He's terrified that it might be too late – that these patterns have become so ingrained that they'll forever define him. But he's willing to take a chance, driven by the hope that he can rediscover the compassionate, connected person he once was, and find some measure of peace after all these years.
